pages.title: About
pages.content:
A small agency for two-room meetings

Koe Interpreters was founded in 2011 and works from Havenkade 14 in Rotterdam. We staff conference booths for bilingual meetings: a roster of thirty-eight conference interpreters covering English, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, French and German.

We only accept assignments where the team can be briefed with documents and terminology in advance. Every language pair gets one booth and two interpreters, and the pair changes turns every thirty minutes.

Request a team →

pages.title: Briefs
pages.content:
Which meetings a brief suits

Which meetings a brief suits: board and investor meetings, press conferences and trade delegations, policy round tables, engineering reviews, cross-border plenaries, factory visits and medical symposia. Send the dates, venue, language pairs and agenda, and we reply within one business day.

Request a team →

pages.title: Meeting day
pages.content:
One booth, two voices

A meeting day starts at 07:45 with a glossary read-through, 08:15 sound check with the technician, 09:00 plenary opens with turns every thirty minutes, 12:30 lunch and handover notes, and 17:30 close with the glossary notes filed by the chief interpreter.

Request a team →

pages.title: Rates
pages.content:
Rates, per interpreter

Prices in EUR, excluding VAT and travel. A one-day bilingual board meeting: 2 interpreters × €1,180 + 2 × €240 preparation = €2,840. The full price table is on the home page.

Request a team →

pages.title: Request a team
pages.content:
Send us the brief

Send us your dates and times, venue or online platform, required language pairs and working agenda to requests@koe-interpreters.example. Our desk at Havenkade 14 in Rotterdam is open Monday to Friday, 08:30–18:00 CET. For urgent requirements within 72 hours, call +31 10 555 0140.

pages.title: Early access
pages.content:
The online brief, spring 2027

The online brief opens in spring 2027. Join the list to upload slides, select room layouts and receive fixed quotes directly: early@koe-interpreters.example.

pages.title: Thank you
pages.content: Your brief is with the desk. We reply within one business day.

pages.title: Privacy
pages.content: We use the details you send with a brief only to answer it and to staff the assignment. We do not sell them and do not share them outside the interpreting team. Ask the request desk to delete your brief at any time.

pages.title: Terms
pages.content: Rates are in EUR, excluding VAT and travel, and are valid for meetings booked from 1 January 2027. Cancellation more than 14 days before the meeting is free; 7 to 14 days, 50%; under 7 days, 100%.

categories.name: Stories
categories.description: Three fixed cases from the booth.

posts.title: What the sound check is for
posts.excerpt: Why a dedicated line check thirty minutes before opening prevents listening fatigue and protects speech clarity.
posts.content:
At 08:15 the technician and the interpreters meet at the booth door. Each interpreter speaks a few lines into the headset while the technician listens on the floor channel and on the relay channel.

The point is not the equipment alone. A clean line means the audience does not strain to follow, and the interpreter does not push the voice to be heard. Thirty minutes of checking saves the whole day from listening fatigue.

We also use the time to agree the hand signals between the two interpreters in the booth, and to confirm which channel carries the relay language.

posts.title: Consecutive notes, explained
posts.excerpt: How structured symbols and vertical margins capture meaning and emphasis during unamplified bilateral talks.
posts.content:
Consecutive interpreters do not write down words. They write down ideas: arrows for cause and result, circles for topics, a line for a change of speaker.

The page is divided by a vertical margin so that links between ideas stay visible. When the speaker pauses, the interpreter reads the page like a map and speaks it back in the other language.

It is a small-room method: bilateral talks, site visits and dinners, where a booth would be out of place.

posts.title: Two days, one board: an EN ⇄ JA meeting
posts.excerpt: A shipping group held a two-day board meeting in English and Japanese; the team was briefed a week ahead.
posts.content:
A shipping group asked for a two-day board meeting in English and Japanese. The documents arrived five working days before, and the glossary was shared two days before the meeting.

On the day the two interpreters alternated every thirty minutes. The resting colleague kept the figures and names. The chief interpreter filed the glossary notes within two business days.

posts.title: Three languages through one relay: a medical symposium
posts.excerpt: A medical-device association needed three languages in one hall; the third booth worked through English relay.
posts.content:
A medical-device association held a symposium in Chinese, English and German. We added a booth and worked through English relay.

Terminology was the main work: the speakers sent their slides early, and the interpreters built one shared glossary for all three booths.

posts.title: A press conference at 48 hours’ notice
posts.excerpt: A consumer-electronics maker called the urgent line for an English and Chinese press conference two days ahead.
posts.content:
A consumer-electronics maker called the urgent line with a press conference in English and Chinese two days away. The desk confirmed a team the same afternoon.

There was time for one call with the speakers and a short glossary. The conference ran to plan.
